name: Southern Tshwa
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Lexical data show that this language has three tone levels: High (H), Mid (M), and Low (L), with the following surface tone melodies: [HH, HM, HL, MM, MH, ML]. [p. 1] ... We posit three underlying tones, High, Mid and Low, to adequately account for the observed melodies. Thus, the two-level melodies with the underlying tones /H/ or /M/, reflect the multiple association of one tone to two morae in a bimoraic root. For instance, the High-level melody is interpreted as having one H tone linked to the first mora while spreading to the second. The three falling melodies associate sequences of two successive tones, one tone linked to each mora in a root. [p. 6]
new_statements.citation: Mathes, Timothy K. & Andy Monthusi Chebanne. 2018. High tone lowering and raising in Tsua. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 54: 1-16. doi:10.5842/54-0-772
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tsua is a lexical tone language with three tone levels (H, M, L) and six root melodies (HH, HM, HL, MM, MH, ML) carried by the two morae of a bimoraic root; root-initial H is lowered after voiced obstruents, aspirated obstruents and /h/, and H is raised to super-high on the high vowels i, u. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be read.
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal: LL, LM and LH melodies unattested in the Tsua data set (p. 7); depression is 'non-systematic' in places (Chebanne 2014: 12). Nothing on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on bimoraic roots (CVV, CVN, CVCV), elicited in citation form from three elderly female speakers; the paper treats the root as the tonal domain and does not discuss stress, prominence, or phrase-level accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kuaa1238 Southern Tshwa [tyu] covers three dialects: Cua/Cuaa (cuat1240), Kua (kuaa1239) and Tsua (tsua1234). The quoted source (Mathes & Chebanne 2018) describes Tsua (tsua1234), spoken in eastern Botswana, from three elderly female speakers; Glottolog's own record for Mathes 2015 assigns Tsua = Southern Tshwa [tyu]. Chebanne 2014 (saved) covers Kua, Cua and Tsua together and calls them a dialect continuum with G|ui/G||ana. Northern Tshwa (tsoa1238; Fehn & Phiri 2017 saved) and Thabala Tchoe (Pratchett 2020 saved) are related Tshwa-complex lects, not this language.

sources.citation: Mathes, Timothy K. & Andy Monthusi Chebanne. 2018. High tone lowering and raising in Tsua. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 54: 1-16. doi:10.5842/54-0-772
sources.quote: Lexical data show that this language has three tone levels: High (H), Mid (M), and Low (L), with the following surface tone melodies: [HH, HM, HL, MM, MH, ML]. [p. 1] ... We posit three underlying tones, High, Mid and Low, to adequately account for the observed melodies. Thus, the two-level melodies with the underlying tones /H/ or /M/, reflect the multiple association of one tone to two morae in a bimoraic root. For instance, the High-level melody is interpreted as having one H tone linked to the first mora while spreading to the second. sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent (the words do not occur). Describes Tsua as a three-level tone language (H, M, L) with six root melodies HH, HM, HL, MM, MH, ML on bimoraic roots (CVV, CVN, CVCV), plus consonant-triggered High Tone Lowering and vowel-triggered High Tone Raising; data are citation forms from three speakers (pp. 1, 2, 6-7).
Secondary, uncited detail: 'There are two tones, high and low, plus a few cases of mid tone' (contradicts the three-level analysis in Mathes & Chebanne 2018); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Chebanne, Andy. 2014. What have Eastern Kalahari Khoe languages lost linguistically? Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 44: 1-21. doi:10.5842/44-0-639
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 3.5 Tone (pp. 11-12): 'The Eastern Kalahari Khoe languages make six tonal distinctions' (HH, HM, HL, LH, MM, LL) shared by Kua, Cua, Tsua with G|ui; tonal depression after voiced/aspirated consonants in Tsua and Cua, not in Kua.
